Use emberdays with your own daily data

Source: vignettes/your-own-data.Rmd
your-own-data.Rmd

The app answers one question about fire-season heat in seven cities. The functions behind it work on any daily series: your own weather station, a Bureau of Meteorology download, river heights or rainfall. This guide shows the three steps.

Step Function What it does
1. Count count_exceedances() Days at or above (or at or below) a threshold, in each year or season, with a missing-data check
2. Compare compare_periods() Average counts in an early and a recent period, using complete seasons only
3. Explain describe_change() One plain-English sentence for a report or a non-specialist 
library(emberdays)
library(dplyr)
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.5.3
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

Your data, your column names

You need one row per day for a single place, with a Date column and a numeric column. The names can be anything. Here a slice of the packaged data stands in for a file you imported, with column names of your own:

my_station <- fire_season_temps |>
  filter(city == "Adelaide") |>
  select(day = date, tmax = max_temp)

head(my_station)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   day         tmax
#>   <date>     <dbl>
#> 1 1910-01-02  37.9
#> 2 1910-01-03  37.4
#> 3 1910-01-04  37.9
#> 4 1910-01-05  39.3
#> 5 1910-01-06  38.2
#> 6 1910-01-07  37.4

If your dates are text, convert them first with as.Date().

1. Count: choose the threshold, the direction and the season

Count summer days (December to February) of 40°C or more. Summer crosses New Year, so start_month = 12 keeps each summer together, labelled like "2018-19":

hot40 <- count_exceedances(my_station, "tmax", threshold = 40, date = "day",
                           start_month = 12, months = c(12, 1, 2))
tail(hot40)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   season_start season  days_possible days_recorded coverage n_exceed extreme
#>          <int> <chr>           <int>         <int>    <dbl>    <int>   <dbl>
#> 1         2013 2013-14            90            90        1       13    45.1
#> 2         2014 2014-15            90            90        1        4    44.1
#> 3         2015 2015-16            91            91        1        7    43.2
#> 4         2016 2016-17            90            90        1        6    42.4
#> 5         2017 2017-18            90            90        1        7    44.1
#> 6         2018 2018-19            90            90        1       10    47.7
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: complete <lgl>
  • n_exceed is the count of days meeting the threshold; extreme is the hottest day.
  • coverage and complete show how much of each season has a reading. Incomplete seasons are kept and flagged, not dropped silently.

Use direction = "below" for the opposite end, for example mild summer days with a maximum of 22°C or less:

mild <- count_exceedances(my_station, "tmax", threshold = 22,
                          direction = "below", date = "day",
                          start_month = 12, months = c(12, 1, 2))

Common season settings:

Season start_month months
Calendar year 1 1:12
Southern fire season 9 c(9:12, 1:2)
Southern summer 12 c(12, 1, 2)
July–June (financial or water year) 7 1:12

2. Compare two periods 

hot_change <- compare_periods(hot40, early = c(1910, 1939),
                              recent = c(1988, 2017))
hot_change
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   period first_season last_season seasons_used mean_hot_days enough_data
#>   <chr>         <int>       <int>        <int>         <dbl> <lgl>      
#> 1 Early          1910        1939           30          2.23 TRUE       
#> 2 Recent         1988        2017           30          4.1  TRUE

enough_data is FALSE when a period has fewer than 10 complete seasons, so you know when an average is fragile.

3. Explain it in one sentence 

describe_change(hot_change, what = "summer days of 40°C or more",
                place = "Adelaide")
#> [1] "In Adelaide, summer days of 40°C or more have become more common: recent seasons (1988–2017) averaged 4.1 per season, compared with 2.2 in 1910–1939, an increase of 1.9 per season (1.8 times the early average)."

mild |>
  compare_periods(early = c(1910, 1939), recent = c(1988, 2017)) |>
  describe_change(what = "mild summer days (22°C or less)", place = "Adelaide")
#> [1] "In Adelaide, mild summer days (22°C or less) have become less common: recent seasons (1988–2017) averaged 9.0 per season, compared with 11.9 in 1910–1939, a decrease of 2.9 per season (0.8 times the early average)."

Paste the sentence into a report, a Quarto document or a Shiny app; the Ember Days app uses exactly this function for its “Answer” line.

Plot the counts

The output is an ordinary tibble, so it plots directly with ggplot2:

library(ggplot2)
#> Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.3

hot40 |>
  filter(complete) |>
  ggplot(aes(season_start, n_exceed)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#C46A1F") +
  labs(x = "Summer (year it starts)", y = "Days of 40°C or more",
       title = "Adelaide summer days of 40°C or more") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")

Things to check first

  • One place at a time. count_exceedances() stops if it finds repeated dates, which usually means two stations are mixed together.
  • Gaps. Look at coverage before trusting a count; the min_coverage argument sets the cut-off (90% by default).
  • Thresholds are yours to justify. Pick a value that means something to your reader, such as a public health heat threshold or a local rainfall benchmark.
